routes.description: Establish that religious faith is an unsupported human projection which adds no necessary explanation of existence, freedom, morality, or meaning, and that appeals to divine authority can displace independent reasoning while intensifying coercion and conflict.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if natural inquiry and human ethical reflection adequately address the phenomena offered for faith, while religious claims remain evidentially unwarranted or produce authority-dependent harms relevant to the motion.

motionBridge.description: Connect the epistemic, moral, and social critiques to the conclusion that faith replaces reason with projection, authority, or harmful consolation rather than revealing God, moral meaning, and human freedom.

centralBridges.description: Show that cosmology, evolution, consciousness, and human experience do not require a personal or interventionist deity as their explanation.
Show that moral judgment and conduct remain available without faith and require context-sensitive reasoning rather than asserted divine absolutes.
Show how scriptural privilege and claims of divine mandate can authorize coercion, institutional abuse, tribal exclusion, or intensified violence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain religious belief and consolation through human psychological needs while distinguishing emotional usefulness from truth.
Provide naturalistic accounts of contingency, transcendence, meaning, and agency sufficient to resist an inference to immaterial divine grounding.

routes.description: Establish that faith reasonably discloses a transcendent source of existence, objective goodness, purposeful meaning, and genuine freedom, while an evolving Jewish tradition can orient conduct toward justice without being reduced to its historical abuses.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if materialism leaves important features of existence, consciousness, moral obligation, meaning, or agency inadequately grounded, and if religious development and practice answer the claim that faith is inherently irrational or harmful.

motionBridge.description: Connect the positive account of transcendence and religious practice to the conclusion that faith can reveal God, moral meaning, and human freedom rather than merely replacing reason.

centralBridges.description: Show why existence, consciousness, love, meaning, or recurrent awareness of God reasonably indicate a transcendent ground beyond material description.
Show that universally binding moral obligation requires a transcendent foundation while remaining compatible with interpretation and ethical reasoning.
Show that intentional human choice cannot be reduced to genetics, environment, determinism, or randomness and therefore requires an immaterial dimension.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how a humanly transmitted religious tradition can refine inherited teachings while continuing to direct adherents toward justice and character development.
Show how religious practice, sanctity, community, and consolation supply purpose and moral motivation without treating practical benefit alone as proof.

sections.title: God, Scientific Inquiry, and Natural Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether existence, cosmic origins, consciousness, love, and recurrent awareness of God warrant a transcendent personal source, or whether natural explanation, uncertainty, and the distinction between a first cause and a religious deity defeat that inference.

sections.title: Human Freedom, Materialism, and Intentional Agency
sections.rationale: The motion expressly concerns human freedom, making it necessary to examine whether genetics and environment exhaust agency, whether contingency or randomness answers determinism, and whether an immaterial ground clarifies intentional choice.

sections.title: Moral Grounding and Ethical Reasoning
sections.rationale: The competing burdens require comparison between transcendent moral obligation and human ethical reflection, including whether unbelievers possess sufficient moral reasons and whether divine commands secure objectivity or complicate contextual judgment.

sections.title: Meaning, Sanctity, Mortality, and Consolation
sections.rationale: Claims about purposeful life, transcendent experience, religious motivation, grief, and consolation bear directly on whether faith reveals genuine meaning or projects reassuring interpretations onto natural human experiences.

sections.title: Religious Tradition, Authority, Reform, and Harm
sections.rationale: This issue joins the dispute over scripture, evolving tradition, charity, institutional authority, proselytism, exclusion, and violence to determine whether religion principally cultivates justice or gives human prejudice and conflict added divine force.

moves.proposition: Human limitations constrain descriptions of God, who is best understood as the source of existence, a relational presence, and the ground of purposeful life.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly addresses the Rabbi, and the sustained first-person answer continues until the moderator turns to Hitchens.

moves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
moves.proposition: Modern cosmology and evolution offer verifiable natural accounts of existence, while cosmic destruction, biological waste, and extinction count against a providential religious plan.
moves.attributionBasis: Wolpe yields the floor, after which Hitchens recommends a physicist, develops the cosmological and evolutionary argument, and concludes with a critique of providence.

components.text: The decisive inference is that unexplained existence and significant intangible phenomena make a purposive theistic explanation reasonable.
The additional demand is whether a source of existence is also warranted as a purposeful relational God.

response.rationale: The reply identifies natural cosmology and evolution as rival explanations and treats extinction and destruction as counterevidence to providential purpose, stating why the theistic inference is unnecessary and strained.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly attacks both explanatory necessity and providential inference, although it does not separately analyze consciousness or love.

precisionFindings.rationale: The natural-explanation and anti-providence claims remain distinct and clear, with an express concession that the plan cannot be disproved.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The explicit inability-to-disprove concession appropriately limits the conclusion to evidential pressure against providential planning rather than certainty.

charity.alternative: Extinction and cosmic destruction could form part of a larger divine plan.
charity.decisiveQualification: Logical compatibility alone does not explain why such waste and destruction should increase confidence in providence.

moves.speaker: Rabbi David Wolpe
moves.proposition: Material causes cannot account for directed human choice, because genetics and environment are given conditions, so free will requires an immaterial dimension grounded in God.
moves.attributionBasis: After a brief exchange, Wolpe begins with a direct rebuttal of Hitchens and develops the first-person free-will challenge until addressing Hitchens at the close.

components.text: Whether verifiable natural cosmology and evolution remove the explanatory need for a providential deity.
Whether belief in God is better explained as fear-driven parental projection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it develops a central contrary consideration but leaves the targeted moves' decisive claims untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The deterministic challenge and proposed immaterial solution are clear, but no qualification explains why immaterial causation escapes the same antecedent-cause problem.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given genetics and environment do not exhaust all causal possibilities, the categorical claim that freedom requires immateriality and God exceeds the supplied warrant.

moves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
moves.proposition: Evolution and genetics include contingency and random mutation rather than complete predetermination, so a material account of human origins does not itself eliminate freedom.
moves.attributionBasis: Hitchens immediately labels the preceding argument and answers it through a sustained discussion of evolutionary contingency, genetics, medicine, and Genesis.

components.text: Whether material human origins entail complete predetermination and therefore require immaterial God-grounded agency.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies the premise of complete predetermination by invoking random mutation and evolutionary contingency, but it does not explain how contingency becomes intentional control.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive determinism premise but leaves the separate demand for an account of directed choice unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anti-predetermination point is clear, but random mutation and freedom are insufficiently distinguished and population-level contingency is extended toward individual agency.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evolutionary contingency refutes a simple fixed blueprint, but the move overstates what randomness establishes about personal freedom and intentional control.

charity.alternative: Random mutation may defeat strict predetermination without producing intentional freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: Indeterminacy and agency are distinct explanatory requirements.

moves.proposition: Judaism centrally directs people toward justice, character refinement, and decent treatment despite abuses committed by religious authorities.
moves.attributionBasis: The response begins with Wolpe answering the scriptural challenge and continues through his direct accusation of asymmetrical reasoning.

A further demand concerns whether natural explanations and destructive history undermine providential religious purpose.

response.rationale: The claims about Judaism's ethical orientation bear on the motion's assessment of religion, but they do not contact the earlier locked projection or natural-explanation demands.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited exegetical purpose supports an ethical orientation, but it is insufficient to establish the dominant effect of an entire diverse tradition.

charity.alternative: Religious ethical teachings can coexist with authoritative texts and institutions that license serious harm.
charity.decisiveQualification: A central aspiration toward goodness does not by itself show that harmful authority is incidental rather than structurally enabled.

components.text: The decisive claim is that Judaism's central ethical purpose adequately distinguishes the tradition from abuses committed under religious authority.

response.rationale: The reply argues that the defects appear within foundational laws themselves, not merely in later abuses, and states the consequence that scripture reflects inherited human prejudice rather than unique divinity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly attacks the premise separating ethical essence from abuse by locating exclusion and hierarchy in the authoritative foundation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited legal features support human historical influence, but the broad inference to scripture generally requires more representative treatment and interpretation.

charity.alternative: An exegetical tradition can reinterpret inherited texts toward justice and character refinement.

moves.speaker: Rabbi David Wolpe
moves.proposition: Religious traditions are humanly transmitted and historically evolving systems capable of refining themselves and discarding inherited moral defects.
moves.attributionBasis: Wolpe is addressed by name at the transition and answers with a continuous account of scriptural formation and social evolution.

components.text: Whether inherited scriptural defects establish religion's enduring moral character and negate its capacity to direct justice.

response.rationale: The reply accepts human transmission and historical defects but argues that interpretation and social evolution can refine them, directly contacting the enduring-authority inference.

moves.speaker: Rabbi David Wolpe
moves.proposition: Religious community and belief in meaning provide profound, nontrivial consolation amid death and grief, even when that meaning cannot be empirically proved.
moves.attributionBasis: Wolpe contrasts Hitchens’s temperament with pastoral experience and sustains the response through his explicit acknowledgment of empirical limits.

moves.proposition: Religion intensifies ordinary tribal and political conflict by adding claims of divine mandate, thereby multiplying violence and making compromise more difficult.

moves.speaker: Christopher Hitchens
moves.proposition: Reciprocal moral rules recur across societies, but difficult cases remain context-sensitive, and contradictory divine absolutes cannot replace the necessary work of ethical reasoning.

routes.description: Defend the evidential force of Grim Reaper paradoxes for causal finitism through a warranted modal-independence principle, while arguing that suffering does not favor indifference once consciousness, background knowledge, human epistemic limits, and morally valuable features of finite life are included.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the modal bridge from a possible infinite causal past to the contradictory arrangement survives the recombination objections, and if the existence and distribution of suffering are shown to be no more expected under indifference than under a suitably specified perfect-being theism.

motionBridge.description: Establish both that Grim Reaper reasoning provides support for causal finitism and that suffering does not yield the proposed comparative advantage for indifference over theism.

centralBridges.description: Justify the conditional from a possible infinite causal history, together with independently variable clock settings, to the possibility of the contradictory Grim Reaper configuration.
Fix the relevant background knowledge and compare how theism and indifference account for consciousness, suffering generally, and the particular observed forms of suffering.

Show how limited human access to divine reasons and goods involving risk, relationship, growth, and finite agency can make unexplained suffering compatible with the expectations of perfect-being theism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish adjacent-world variation of jointly existing objects from unrestricted infinite recombination and explain why the former retains evidential force.
Supply a morally relevant account of divine permission, including the possible roles of consent, compensation, responsibility, and world-level goods.

routes.description: Block the inference from Grim Reaper contradictions to causal finitism by locating the inconsistency in the arrangement rather than the infinite past, while defending the modest likelihood claim that severe apparently gratuitous suffering is more expected under indifference than under bare perfect-being theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if an infinite causal past need not license the paradoxical recombination and the minimal inconsistency diagnosis is adequate, and if the observed severity and distribution of suffering remain comparatively less expected under theism after the proposed background assumptions and theodicies are examined.

motionBridge.description: Establish both that Grim Reaper paradoxes do not support causal finitism and that observed suffering supplies comparative evidence favoring indifference over perfect-being theism.

centralBridges.description: Show that rejecting only the jointly inconsistent Grim Reaper conditions blocks the paradox without requiring rejection of every infinite causal history.
Demonstrate that infinite recombination and proximity intuitions do not reliably transmit possibility to the paradoxical total configuration.
Show that the severity, apparent gratuity, and unequal distribution of suffering lower its expected probability under bare perfect-being theism relative to indifference.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why the logically minimal inconsistency diagnosis is preferable to adding a substantive causal-finitist restriction when both exclude the paradox.
Test whether skeptical-theist and purpose-specific explanations have independent grounding and preserve meaningful confirmation and disconfirmation by worldly evidence.

sections.title: Grim Reaper Contradiction and the Causal-Finitist Inference
sections.rationale: This issue contains the direct motion-level dispute over whether the contradiction warrants rejecting an infinite causal past or only the jointly unsatisfiable features of the proposed arrangement.

sections.title: Modal Independence, Recombination, and Possibility
sections.rationale: The causal-finitist argument depends on a defensible transition from possible components or nearby configurations to the possibility of the infinite paradoxical whole.

sections.title: Comparative Likelihoods and Evidential Background
sections.rationale: The suffering dispute turns on how theism and indifference predict consciousness, suffering in general, and its specific observed forms once shared background knowledge and auxiliary commitments are fixed.

sections.title: Unknown Reasons, Moral Knowledge, and Evidential Symmetry
sections.rationale: Appeals to cognitive limitation must be weighed against ordinary moral knowledge and the concern that unrestricted unknown-purpose explanations neutralize evidence both against and for divine goodness.

sections.title: Theodicies and the Severity and Distribution of Suffering
sections.rationale: Consent, compensation, finite-agent goods, relationships, and world-level value must address not merely suffering's possibility but its extreme cases, unequal allocation, and apparently better alternatives.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative evidential route from the intelligibility of nature and mathematics, historically grounded miracle claims, moral experience, and the Christian treatment of evil toward rationally warranted Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: Show that these considerations jointly fit Christian theism better than agnostic naturalism, while defending evidence-based faith, the coherence of divine action, and grounds for trusting divine goodness despite suffering.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative force of scientific, mathematical, historical, moral, and existential considerations to an evidence-based commitment to Christian theism.

centralBridges.description: Explain why the intelligibility of nature and the effectiveness of mathematics are expected if a rational divine mind grounds both the cosmos and human reason.
Establish that Christian faith can be a reasoned commitment grounded in cumulative historical, experiential, and inferential evidence rather than unsupported assent.
Defend the epistemic coherence and historical importance of real divine miracles as signs disclosing the identity and purposes of Christ.
Account for moral evil through significant freedom and connect the cross, resurrection, judgment, and restoration to trust and hope amid suffering.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish successful methodological naturalism within science from the broader metaphysical claim that naturalism exhausts rational explanation.
Show how the theological meaning of Gospel narratives can depend upon, and be strengthened by, the reality of the events they report.

routes.description: Establish a cautious nonbelieving route by separating methodological science from theological explanation, distinguishing faith from empirical inference, interpreting miracle narratives without requiring supernatural events, and treating innocent suffering as evidence against confidence in a good God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the offered considerations do not warrant the specifically Christian conclusion because naturalistic inquiry does not require God, religious meaning can remain faith-based or nonliteral, and severe evil resists the proposed account of divine goodness.

motionBridge.description: Demonstrate that scientific order, religious experience, miracle narratives, and proposed answers to evil underdetermine the move from philosophical possibility to evidence-based Christian faith.

centralBridges.description: Explain why science may have Christian historical roots yet operate successfully through methodological naturalism without using God as an explanatory component.
Maintain a distinction between empirically supported scientific inference and the faith commitments through which Christian experience and doctrine are interpreted.
Offer an account of Gospel miracle narratives centered on moral, communal, and religious meaning without requiring supernatural violations or physically demonstrated events.
Show why the scale of innocent suffering and the costs imposed on victims challenge both the free-will defense and an evidential inference to divine goodness.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test natural-theology inferences by raising questions about the explanatory status of a designer and the evidential significance of defective features in creation.
Allow ultimate metaphysical questions and theological proposals while requiring that they remain distinct from scientific conclusions and open to criticism.

sections.title: Science, Mathematics, and the Intelligibility of Nature
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the historical origins, rational order, and mathematical tractability of science support a divine mind or remain compatible with methodologically naturalistic inquiry.

sections.title: Faith, Evidence, and Natural-Theology Inference
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether Christian commitment can arise from cumulative publicly assessable reasons or instead depends on a prior framework of faith that organizes experience and interpretation.

sections.title: Miracle Claims, Historical Reality, and Gospel Meaning
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether resurrection and Gospel signs function as coherent historical evidence of Christ or carry their religious significance without literal supernatural occurrence.

sections.title: Evil, Human Freedom, and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether atrocities and innocent suffering defeat confidence in a good God or can be situated within freedom, divine participation, final justice, and restoration.

sections.title: Science, Metaphysics, and Explanatory Limits
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies whether science's methodological boundaries leave rational space for theological explanation while avoiding an unwarranted transition from scientific practice to either theism or metaphysical naturalism.

routes.description: Establish that human beings knowingly violate a binding divine moral law, justly face judgment, and can receive mercy because Christ bears the consequence of sin, with repentance and trust supplying the stated route to salvation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the account connects personal guilt to deserved judgment, explains why Christ's substitution permits mercy without abandoning justice, and supplies a coherent basis for accepting the promised salvation through repentance and faith.

motionBridge.description: Show that the gospel forms a morally and explanatorily coherent sequence from sin and judgment through substitutionary atonement to salvation.

centralBridges.description: Ground personal guilt and accountability in a divine moral law disclosed through conscience and manifested in human wrongdoing.
Explain why death and final judgment are proportionate consequences of sin under the authority and goodness attributed to God.
Explain how Christ's sacrificial death and resurrection can satisfy justice while making divine mercy available to guilty people.
Connect repentance and trust in Christ, rather than moral works, to forgiveness, transformation, and eternal life.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply a basis for treating scripture, creation, conscience, or claimed religious experience as warrant for the gospel's premises.
Account for suffering, unbelief, apostasy, and religious disagreement without severing the proposed sequence of guilt, atonement, and salvation.

routes.description: Show that the gospel's allocation of responsibility, model of punishment and substitution, salvation mechanism, or supporting epistemology fails to provide a morally defensible and reliably grounded explanation of sin, atonement, and salvation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if central gospel premises are shown to depend on unjust responsibility transfer, unnecessary or ineffective sacrifice, disproportionate judgment, or claims whose truth and promised operation cannot be independently tested.

motionBridge.description: Show that one or more indispensable links in the gospel's account lack moral justification or explanatory coherence.

centralBridges.description: Test whether personal or inherited guilt remains justly attributable when an omniscient creator deliberately selects the conditions producing sin and unbelief.
Test whether substitutionary sacrifice is necessary, morally legitimate, and capable of addressing wrongdoing rather than merely transferring its cost.
Test whether final punishment and the conditions for salvation are proportionate, coherent, and consistent with divine power and foreknowledge.
Require publicly defensible grounds for divine authority, scripture, resurrection, and promised salvation that can distinguish truth from private conviction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide a consequence-sensitive account of moral judgment against which divine-command definitions of sin and punishment can be examined.
Use suffering, religious disagreement, apostasy, and dependence of personality on the brain to test supporting theological explanations.

sections.title: Moral law, sin, and personal accountability
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether conscience and human wrongdoing establish culpable sin, and whether responsibility remains personal given inherited guilt, situational morality, and divine foreknowledge or world selection.

sections.title: Judgment, suffering, and divine goodness
sections.rationale: The moral sense of the gospel depends on whether death, hell, and suffering can be reconciled with proportionate justice, divine goodness, and the creator's responsibility for foreseeable conditions.

sections.title: Necessity and moral logic of substitutionary atonement
sections.rationale: Christ's sacrificial payment is the central transition from guilt to mercy, making its necessity, legitimacy, and capacity to address the wrongdoer indispensable to the motion.

sections.title: Conditions and efficacy of salvation
sections.rationale: This issue covers whether repentance and faith rather than works coherently secure forgiveness and transformation, and whether the promised mechanism can accommodate unsuccessful seekers, apostasy, and divine foreknowledge.

sections.title: Evidence, revelation, and warranted trust
sections.rationale: The account's explanatory force depends on warranted access to its premises, including God's existence and authority, scripture, resurrection, and religious experience, rather than assumptions insulated from independent testing.

routes.description: Establish that Catholic theism can reconcile hiddenness, unequal religious conditions, sincere nonbelief, hell, and original sin with universal grace by combining providential formation, meaningful creaturely agency, differentiated goods, and humanity's recoverable loss of gratuitous gifts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if universal access to sufficient grace remains coherent despite unequal explicit revelation, responsible refusal remains possible without treating belief as directly voluntary, and inherited fallen conditions can be explained without attributing arbitrary punishment or divine abandonment.

motionBridge.description: Show that grace, providence, and creaturely agency jointly explain the motion's apparent counterevidence without denying its unequal and painful manifestations.

centralBridges.description: Account for sincere nonbelief and religious geography while maintaining that every person receives a genuinely sufficient path toward God.
Explain how providentially supplied opportunities can coexist with finite interpretation, temporal development, contingency, and meaningful refusal.
Explain original sin as the loss of gratuitous gifts through shared human rejection while preserving the availability of restoration.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Relate unequal natural, cultural, and revelatory conditions to differentiated personal and communal goods rather than uniform distribution.
Show how scriptural narrative and suffering can form receptivity to revelation within a larger providential history.

routes.description: Establish that persistent sincere nonbelief, culturally patterned revelation, unequal salvific costs, hell, and inherited fallen conditions are less expected under a loving God who seeks relationship with everyone than under explanations centered on human culture and contingency.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed appeals to grace, providence, agency, differentiated goods, and original sin do not adequately explain failed divine contact, unequal access and eternal stakes, rationally involuntary rejection, or inherited deprivation following deception.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined pattern of hiddenness, unequal geography, sincere nonbelief, hell, and original sin counts against Catholic theism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that sincere seekers can remain without reciprocal divine contact despite willingness to know and relate to God.
Connect geographic and social disparities in revelation to unequal intellectual, practical, and potentially eternal consequences.
Challenge whether nonbelief, rejection of salvation, or primordial disobedience can bear the required culpability under ignorance, cognitive limitation, or deception.
Challenge whether solidarity with primordial humanity can justify inherited deprivation and suffering for later persons.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether contingent encounters, interrupted lives, and providential orchestration can be reconciled with both fair access and creaturely freedom.
Test whether appeals to a larger divine story explain severe suffering and withheld explanation consistently with divine love.

sections.title: Divine Hiddenness and Sincere Seeking
sections.rationale: This issue tests the central relational question: whether persistent nonbelief among willing seekers is compatible with universal divine availability and a life-spanning process of revelation and formation.

sections.title: Religious Geography, Unequal Access, and Fairness
sections.rationale: This issue connects culturally uneven belief and differing social costs to the competing expectations of universal divine concern, differentiated providence, and sociological transmission.

sections.title: Grace, Responsible Refusal, and Hell
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether sufficient grace and meaningful agency can ground responsibility for rejecting salvation when belief is not directly voluntary and the consequences are eternal.

sections.title: Providence, Mortal Contingency, and Transformative Suffering
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether interrupted lives, contingent encounters, and suffering can belong to a coherent providential history without making access arbitrary or compromising creaturely agency.

sections.title: Original Sin, Deception, Solidarity, and Restoration
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the fall can coherently explain humanity's inherited condition through lost gratuitous gifts and shared nature despite objections concerning deception, culpability, and intergenerational justice.

routes.description: Establish that the surviving witness tradition and comparative methods preserve the New Testament's wording to a sufficiently high, historically appropriate degree of probability for the text to be trusted, despite localized uncertainty and the loss of the autographs.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if cumulative manuscript evidence and reconstructive method justify substantial recovery under a probabilistic standard, while the remaining meaningful variants are shown to be limited enough that local uncertainty does not defeat trust in the text as a whole.

motionBridge.description: Connect substantial probabilistic recovery, rather than certainty at every disputed reading, to the level of confidence required to trust the New Testament text.

centralBridges.description: Show that numerous, early, geographically or genealogically independent manuscripts, versions, and patristic witnesses provide cumulative access to earlier textual states.
Explain how comparison across branching written witnesses can identify copying errors and reconstruct ancestral wording even when the autographs and earliest copies are unavailable.
Establish that most variants are insignificant or readily identifiable and that the smaller set of meaningful viable disputes does not prevent substantial textual recovery.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply concrete evidence of careful early transmission or agreement between early witnesses that supports stability before the principal surviving codices.
Justify probability rather than absolute certainty as the appropriate standard for historical trust and relate the available evidence to ordinary work on ancient texts.

routes.description: Establish that textual criticism may recover an ancestral form behind the surviving witnesses without providing enough evidence to identify that form confidently with the authors' original wording, making the requested level of textual trust unwarranted.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the undocumented earliest transmission period leaves a material possibility of consequential changes shared by all surviving branches, and if later abundance, reconstructive success, or broad continuity cannot close that evidentiary gap to the autograph.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unresolved gap between the earliest reconstructable text and the authorial wording to the conclusion that confidence sufficient for the motion has not been established.

centralBridges.description: Show that the loss of the autographs and earliest generations of copies prevents direct testing of copying accuracy during the period most capable of seeding every surviving branch.
Maintain the distinction between reconstructing the initial ancestor of extant witnesses and demonstrating that this reconstructed text is identical to the autograph.
Establish that scribal variation includes intentional, substantial, or interpretively consequential changes, so recoverable broad continuity does not resolve every material uncertainty.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why the quantity of predominantly later witnesses and the low proportion of significant extant variants do not reveal changes predating the earliest surviving evidence.
Specify why the advocate of trust must provide affirmative evidence of reliable early transmission rather than treat the absence of known total discontinuity as sufficient.

sections.title: The Standard for Recovery and Textual Trust
sections.rationale: This issue defines whether the motion requires autographic certainty or a historically reasonable degree of confidence, and therefore sets the burden against which manuscript evidence and residual uncertainty must be considered.

sections.title: The Undocumented Earliest Transmission Period
sections.rationale: The central historical dispute concerns whether missing originals and early copies leave an unbridgeable evidentiary gap or whether circulation patterns, early witnesses, versions, and patristic testimony support continuity with authorial wording.

sections.title: Reconstructing Earlier Texts from Surviving Witnesses
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether comparison among branching manuscript traditions can recover predecessor readings despite accumulated errors, and whether the earliest reconstructable text can be identified with the autograph.

sections.title: The Evidentiary Value of Manuscript Abundance and Date
sections.rationale: The number, age, independence, and coverage of surviving witnesses matter to whether the manuscript tradition provides effective cross-checks, while raising the question whether relative abundance establishes original wording.

sections.title: The Scale and Proportion of Textual Variation
sections.rationale: This issue separates the raw number of variants from the subset that is meaningful and viable, determining what the surviving variation establishes about the stability and recoverability of the text.

sections.title: Consequential Variants and the Scope of Trust
sections.rationale: Disputed readings and recognized additions test whether local uncertainty materially limits textual trust, including whether interpretive or doctrinal significance bears on confidence in the New Testament as a whole.

routes.description: Establish that consciousness or mind is fundamental by presenting idealism as the more economical explanation of experience, information, causation, and observer-linked quantum phenomena, while supplying an account of physical development and an empirical condition that could undermine the view.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its ontology explains experienced and physical regularities without an indispensable material substrate, connects quantum observation to consciousness without preventing pre-observer development, and identifies a publicly examinable way in which the account could fail.

motionBridge.description: Show that idealism and the cited quantum considerations jointly provide good reason to treat consciousness or a divine mind as fundamental.

centralBridges.description: Establish a cumulative inference from mental correlations, top-down causation, informational structure, and limits of material reduction to an idealist ontology.
Explain how informational evolution and observer-linked definite appearances can accommodate physical interaction and cosmic development before local conscious observers.
State empirical implications or potential defeaters that make the consciousness-dependent account publicly examinable rather than insulated from evidence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the ontology by arguing that experienced properties and informational distinctions do not require an additional material substance.
Clarify what interactions and structures remain as informational evolution when no thinking observer produces definite spatiotemporal appearances.

routes.description: Require independently confirmable manifestations and mind-independent causal interaction for the affirmative claim, distinguish legitimate inference from unsupported ontology, and test whether consciousness-dependent physics explains preconscious development or instead adds an unfalsifiable divine or mental condition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed idealist and quantum inferences lack independently demonstrable support, fail to account for physical interaction and development without observer dependence, or do not yield discriminating empirical consequences sufficient to justify fundamentality.

motionBridge.description: Show that the claim of fundamental consciousness or divine mind fails the relevant public-demonstrability or physical-interaction requirements.

centralBridges.description: Establish that burden-bearing claims require detectable, repeatable, and independently confirmable consequences in shared reality.
Distinguish inferences built from mutually reinforcing demonstrable evidence from an idealist inference whose components may not independently support its ontology.
Account for forces, chemistry, and physical development through causal relations that do not depend on being mentally experienced.
Determine whether observer-dependent reality has a discriminating falsification condition and whether its additional mental commitments perform necessary explanatory work.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test the account against evolution and chemical interaction occurring before ordinary conscious observers were present.
Examine whether informational and video-game analogies entail the claimed absence of definite or maintained unobserved physical structure.

sections.title: Public Evidence and Explanatory Inference
sections.rationale: This issue sets the governing evidential burden and tests whether the affirmative cumulative inference resembles established evidence-based inference closely enough to support a fundamental ontology.

sections.title: Information, Experience, and Material Substrate
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether experienced properties, mathematics, and informational distinctions make matter explanatorily redundant or whether physical properties denote mind-independent causal capacities.

sections.title: Observer Dependence and Preconscious Development
sections.rationale: This issue is central to whether an observer-linked quantum account can accommodate evolution, chemistry, and continuing interaction before local minds without relying on an unexplained divine observer.

sections.title: Unobserved Reality and Physical Interaction
sections.rationale: This issue tests what persists without thinking minds and whether analogies involving rendering or informational evolution support the claimed relation between observation, spacetime definiteness, and causal interaction.

sections.title: Falsifiability and Ontological Parsimony
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether the consciousness-dependent account exposes itself to a discriminating empirical defeater and whether its ontological commitments satisfy the debate's demonstrability and economy requirements.

routes.description: Establish that naturalism can account for mind, intentionality, morality, and ultimate reality through physically grounded but irreducibly useful explanatory levels, evolutionary and cultural processes, public ethical inquiry, and nature itself without an additional transcendent posit.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects physical organization to genuine intentional explanation, supplies a secular basis for moral deliberation, and shows that religious ultimacy adds no sufficiently intelligible or necessary explanatory content beyond the natural world.

motionBridge.description: Show that the phenomena named by the motion are explainable within nature and require no additional religious framework of ultimate reality.

centralBridges.description: Explain how physical realization supports real and causally relevant intentional patterns without requiring a separate mental substance.
Ground moral judgment in corrigible public reasoning and mutual persuasion without granting automatic authority to revelation.
Identify the universe and its laws as ultimate while requiring any proposed transcendent alternative to have intelligible explanatory and epistemic content.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for higher-level human phenomena through design, intentional, evolutionary, and cultural explanations compatible with physical constraint.
Explain how the social functions and institutional effects of religion can be evaluated without treating religious metaphysics as explanatorily necessary.

routes.description: Establish that a broad, science-compatible account should treat subjective and intentional states as real while situating moral life, reflective inquiry, and the natural universe within a substantive religious worldview concerning a deeper ground of reality.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it shows that naturalistic description does not exhaust personhood or ultimacy, articulates a coherent additional metaphysical framework, and demonstrates that this framework remains open to rational discussion and experience-sensitive revision.

motionBridge.description: Show that a religious account supplies a substantive and rationally discussable framework beyond an account that treats nature as exhaustive.

centralBridges.description: Establish that subjective and intentional states are genuine constituents and causes within personhood rather than merely predictive descriptions.
Connect moral community and philosophical inquiry to substantive beliefs about a personal or deeper ground in which experienced reality participates.
Specify the universe as contained within a broader ultimate reality and identify how that ontological claim differs from naturalistic ultimacy.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve the explanatory resources of physical, biological, and human sciences while allowing their subject matters distinct causal significance.
Show that religious commitments can oppose fanaticism, remain answerable to reason, and change in response to relevant experience.

sections.title: Physical Constraint and Higher-Level Causation
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether design-level and intentional explanations can be both physically realized and genuinely causal, or whether explanatory pluralism requires stronger ontological standing for higher-level causes.

sections.title: Subjective Experience, Mental Reality, and Personhood
sections.rationale: The treatment of subjective states bears directly on whether organized physical systems exhaust mentality and whether first-person experience remains an indispensable constituent of agency and persons.

sections.title: Moral Grounding and the Public Role of Religion
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether morality is adequately grounded in secular, revisable deliberation and how religious communities, commitments, and practices relate to reason, altruism, and harmful forms of belief.

sections.title: Content and Epistemic Accountability of Religious Claims
sections.rationale: A religious framework can add explanatory force only if its claims possess distinguishable content and conditions for rational or experiential revision rather than remaining insulated by appeals to mystery.

sections.title: Nature, Transcendence, and Ultimate Reality
sections.rationale: The motion-level disagreement turns on whether the universe and its laws exhaust reality or instead participate in a broader ground whose metaphysical role constitutes an additional explanatory framework.

moves.speaker: Philip Clayton
moves.proposition: Broad naturalism should draw on the distinct explanatory resources of physical, biological, and human sciences according to the phenomena under investigation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Clayton the opening turn, and the uninterrupted first-person exposition continues until Dennett answers.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Physical law constrains action while design-level and intentional-level descriptions remain indispensable explanations of organized systems and agents.
moves.attributionBasis: Clayton's criticism is followed by a sustained first-person clarification using Dennett's characteristic three-stance framework and chess-computer example.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Successful functional organization of physical components suffices for mentality, without any additional mental substance or ectoplasm.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett addresses Clayton by name and gives a direct, sustained clarification of what physical organization must supply for intentional interpretation and mind.

moves.speaker: Philip Clayton

moves.attributionBasis: Dennett addresses Clayton by name and directly questions how Clayton can know that their views differ under the stated epistemic limitations.

moves.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly announces his argument that belief in God plays no necessary role in morality and then develops the secular deliberative alternative.

moves.speaker: Philip Clayton

moves.attributionBasis: Clayton answers a direct question about what would be missing if his outlook were called wholly secular and distinguishes shared ethics from religious worldview commitments.

routes.description: Establish that the modern West's characteristic commitments to compassion, equality, freedom, consent, and abolition are historically unintelligible without Christianity's doctrines, narratives, communities, and institutions, while allowing that Christian influence need not be exclusive or mechanically deterministic.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it identifies distinctively Christian moral ideas, shows credible mechanisms transmitting them into Western practices and institutions, and explains apparent scriptural, ecclesial, and pre-Christian counterexamples without making every Western outcome Christian by definition.

motionBridge.description: Connect the named modern Western values to an indispensable Christian historical genealogy rather than merely showing temporal coexistence or isolated Christian participation.

centralBridges.description: Identify Christian doctrines and narratives capable of generating universal dignity, concern for the weak, reciprocal obligation, and emancipation.
Trace those moral sources through communities, legal concepts, reform movements, and durable institutions into the modern West.
Account for difficult biblical texts, Christian defenses of hierarchy or slavery, and analogous pre-Christian values while preserving the claimed genealogy.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend a bounded historical standard under which inherited influence can persist despite unbelief, contestation, and later secular reformulations.
Explain why proposed material, political, or counterfactual alternatives do not eliminate Christianity's contribution to the history that occurred.

routes.description: Establish that the modern Western moral package is better explained by multiple traditions, institutional conflict, material change, oppressed groups' resistance, and secular moral development, while permitting particular and substantial Christian contributions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it distinguishes Christian contribution from Christian necessity or authorship, supplies credible independent sources and causal mechanisms for the named values, and shows that contrary biblical and Christian precedents limit any uniquely Christian genealogy.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christianity is one contingent contributor within a mixed genealogy rather than the indispensable source of the named modern Western values.

centralBridges.description: Establish that compassion, protection, equality, or related moral practices arose before or outside Christianity in forms relevant to the origin claim.
Explain modern rights and reforms through institutional conflict, self-interest, resistance by oppressed groups, technological change, and material conditions.
Use biblical permissions, exclusions, coercive implications, and competing Christian historical practices to test claims of inherent Christian development.
Separate Christian participation or institutionalization from authorship, uniqueness, necessity, and completion of modern moral principles.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require criteria that distinguish genuine Christian inheritance from retrospective selection of Christian precedents for any eventual Western outcome.
Test the genealogy against the specific modern meanings of freedom, equal social standing, bodily autonomy, and universal abolition.

sections.title: Standards for Historical Moral Genealogy
sections.rationale: The debate depends on what counts as causal inheritance: indispensable influence, unique origin, institutional contribution, or one factor among many. This section covers boundedness, falsifiability, secular reformulation, alternative pathways, and the distinction between actual history and counterfactual development.

sections.title: Compassion, the Weak, and Protective Institutions
sections.rationale: Compassion supplies a principal test of whether Christian narrative and worship generated a distinctive concern for vulnerable people and scaled it through hospitals and charity, or instead institutionalized values already present in other traditions.

sections.title: Rights, Equality, and Freedom
sections.rationale: This section addresses central named and defining Western commitments by testing proposed lines from biblical anthropology, Christian practice, canon law, dissent, and natural rights against founding-era unbelief, exclusion, institutional conflict, and social struggle.

sections.title: Gender Equality, Marriage, and Consent
sections.rationale: Gender equality and bodily autonomy test whether reciprocal Christian teachings and women's early religious roles contain a trajectory toward modern equality and consent, or whether scriptural restrictions and the limits of mutual marital authority require other developments.

sections.title: Scripture, Slavery, and Abolition
sections.rationale: Abolition is a major motion-level case because Christian scripture, churches, enslaved believers, and reformers appear within both emancipatory and pro-slavery histories. The issue tests narrative interpretation, textual permission, institutional transformation, political struggle, and causal attribution.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the pro side's bounded motion-level causal thesis and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

routes.description: Establish a historically usable body of early testimony concerning Jesus' postmortem appearances and bodily resurrection, then show that an intentional divine resurrection explains that evidence more adequately than the proposed natural mechanisms under a defensible method of historical comparison.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early testimony warrants the relevant appearance and bodily-resurrection claims, the resurrection hypothesis supplies the strongest unified explanation of them, and objections based on hallucination, source unreliability, missing-body alternatives, and antecedent improbability do not defeat that inference.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historically warranted appearance and bodily-resurrection evidence to the conclusion that Jesus rose and that this hypothesis better explains the testimony than naturalistic alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Establish that sufficiently early and historically usable sources report individual and group experiences interpreted as appearances of the risen Jesus and as bodily resurrection.
Show that hallucination, visionary contagion, disappearance, fabrication, and related natural proposals do not jointly match the evidence as well as the resurrection hypothesis.

Justify evaluating competing hypotheses through explanatory scope, power, ad hocness, and plausibility while handling disputed prior probabilities without excluding purposive divine action in advance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how physical-body considerations, possible grave investigation, and the early proclaimers' sincere commitment constrain disappearance and fabrication accounts.
Defend the historical usability of the Gospel narrative core despite genre conventions, literary development, and discrepancies in peripheral details.

routes.description: Show that the surviving early testimony is sparse, culturally mediated, and compatible with ordinary processes such as visions, social reinforcement, disappearance, and narrative development, while arguing that its evidential force is insufficient to overcome the resurrection hypothesis's weak antecedent support.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if one or more collectively credible natural processes adequately account for the reported testimony without requiring a uniquely reconstructed history, and if source limitations and prior-probability considerations prevent that testimony from making resurrection the better historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the availability and collective plausibility of natural mechanisms, together with evidential limitations, to rejection of resurrection as the better explanation of early Christian testimony.

centralBridges.description: Establish that religious visions, charismatic suggestion, cultural reinforcement, cognitive processes, and ordinary missing-body scenarios can generate the central reported beliefs and traditions.

Show that a hypothesis involving resurrection requires unusually strong evidence because it lacks established background precedent and depends on prior commitments about divine existence and intention.
Demonstrate that the early epistolary record lacks sufficient detail and that later narrative sources contain features that limit their ability to establish bodily encounters and an empty grave.
Justify historical rejection of resurrection when several collectively likely natural scenarios remain available even if the evidence does not identify one complete natural reconstruction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how sincere believers could infer bodily resurrection without verifying an empty grave or could assimilate contrary physical evidence through prior religious commitments.
Account for the restricted appearance pattern and exceptional conversions as features expected within a localized visionary movement rather than public divine disclosure.

sections.title: Historical Method, Reference Classes, and Prior Probability
sections.rationale: The governing comparison determines whether explanatory criteria may bracket disputed priors or whether resurrection's lack of established precedent imposes an extraordinary evidential threshold; that choice structures every later inference from the testimony.

sections.title: Pauline Testimony and the Bodily Character of Resurrection
sections.rationale: The early Pauline material supplies the principal evidential base for appearances and bodily-resurrection belief, while its chronology, detail, interpretation, and capacity to support physical encounters remain central points of dispute.

sections.title: Visionary, Psychological, and Social-Contagion Explanations
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of individual and group experiences bear directly on whether ordinary religious and social processes can explain the appearance traditions or whether their phenomenology and distribution require a different causal account.

sections.title: Empty Grave, Investigation, and Proclaimer Sincerity
sections.rationale: Questions about disappearance, grave verification, bodily inference, and the costly sincerity of early proclaimers constrain both fabrication accounts and claims that vision-driven belief could develop independently of physical evidence.

sections.title: Historical Usability of the Gospel Narratives
sections.rationale: The status of Gospel detail affects whether empty-tomb and embodied-appearance narratives can supplement the sparse epistolary record, requiring attention to genre, embellishment, literary construction, external support, and contradictions.
